fullDescription: Animate the brand mark for 2-5 seconds - the clip that closes a launch video or opens a demo. Plate-then-animate around a locked mark that is never redrawn: flat marks move their own parts, dimensional marks take light and depth, and every glyph is inspected letter by letter (95% right is 100% wrong). Adapted from Krea's krea-motion skill (MIT).
prompt:
# Logo Sting

Animate the brand mark for two to five seconds: the clip that closes a launch video, opens a demo, or plays on a social post. A logo is the hardest easy request in AI video - every other subject tolerates a little drift, a wordmark does not. One re-lettered character, one warped counter, one shifted kerning pair, and the clip is unusable no matter how beautiful the light is. The whole craft is motion around a mark that is treated as inviolable geometry, never redrawn.

## When to use

- A launch video, demo, or presentation needs an ending or opening beat with the brand mark.
- A social post wants the logo to arrive with some ceremony instead of sitting there.
- The user asks for an "animated logo", "logo animation", "logo reveal", or "sting".

Do not use for: an ambient background behind a headline (use `Video Generation / Hero Loop`), the mark placed in a street scene (use `Video Generation / Billboard Placement`), or creating the mark itself (use `Image Generation / IP as Logo`). If the deliverable needs a tagline, legal line, or any typographic layout beyond the mark, generate the textless sting here and add the type in the page or in post - never ask the video model to invent letterforms.

## First decision: flat or dimensional?

Look at the mark before choosing any treatment. Getting this wrong is what produces the free-template look.

**A flat vector mark** - solid fills, no material, no baked-in lighting - has no surface for light to rake across and nothing to reveal at macro scale. Light sweeps over flat artwork degrade into bars sliding across a logo, the cheapest effect there is. A flat mark animates through its **own parts**: elements displace slightly and snap back into registration, or ignite in color one by one.

**A dimensional mark** - embossed, inlaid metal, printed on a real surface, extruded - has material and depth. Light, shadow, focus, and emergence treatments all work.

A flat mark can become dimensional: render it as a physical object first (brushed metal inlay, embossed paper, soft-touch print) with image generation, approve that still, then animate the dimensional version. That is a plate decision, which is where this starts.

## Two stages, always

**Stage 1 - build the plate.** The sting inherits its composition, background, material, and margins from a still. Start from the user's actual logo file or a mark from `Image Generation / IP as Logo`, and compose the plate with image generation: mark at final position (usually dead center), generous margins, the background it will end on, and the material treatment if the mark is going dimensional. Iterate here, where regeneration is cheap and the mark is guaranteed correct. Do not move to video until the plate would stand on its own as the sting's final frame - because it is.

**Stage 2 - animate.** Feed the plate to video generation and describe motion only.

## The mark is locked

The same doctrine as Billboard Placement, and it costs even more here because the mark fills the frame. Never spell the wordmark, name the brand, or describe the logo's shapes, colors, or letterforms in the motion prompt - the model reads those words as an instruction to redraw the mark, and a redrawn mark is a deformed mark. Refer to it only by position: "the mark at center", "the emblem's separate shapes". State the lock explicitly and end the prompt with it; unprompted, video models love to add a tagline underneath a logo, so ban added text every time.

## Treatments that survive a single clip

One treatment per clip, chosen for the mark you have. Concrete magnitudes keep transforms rigid - "rotates 8 degrees" preserves geometry; "forms", "assembles", or "materializes" invents new geometry.

| Treatment | What moves | What stays locked | For |
|---|---|---|---|
| Displace and snap | Each separate shape shifts a few millimetres or rotates 5–10° apart, holds, then all snap back into exact registration on one frame | Every shape keeps its drawn form; only rigid moves | Flat marks with separable parts - the default |
| Color ignition | Elements light up in their own color one by one, from grayscale or dark | All geometry, all positions | Flat marks, monograms |
| Specular sweep | One hard highlight travels across the mark at a constant rate | Camera and mark completely still | Dimensional marks; the most reliable treatment |
| Shadow retreat | A hard-edged shadow travels off the mark, uncovering it | Camera and mark completely still | Dimensional marks, dramatic openings |
| Depth emergence | The mark rises a few millimetres out of the surface, cast shadow appearing under its edges | Letterforms extrude, never redraw | Dimensional marks on a material ground |

The payoff of displace-and-snap is the click into place: parts must move away and **hold** their offset, so the final snap has somewhere to travel from. Parts that resolve themselves as they go leave dead air at the tail.

Never ask for: letters flying in and assembling (each letter is redrawn in flight), handwriting or draw-on animation (the model invents strokes), morphing between two marks (both end up wrong), liquid or smoke forming the logo, a 3D logo tumbling in space (perspective change re-renders the glyphs), rings or ripples pinging around the mark, or a uniform zoom as the only motion.

## Motion budget

The motion prompt is capped at **500 characters** and describes motion only. Spend it in this order:

1. **The treatment** - what moves, its magnitude, its rate, when it resolves.
2. **The lock** - what never changes: the mark's geometry, and usually the camera.
3. **The exclusions** - no added text, no extra graphics.

Count the characters before sending. If it exceeds 500, cut magnitude detail first - never the lock clause and never the no-added-text clause.

## Model and resolution

| Model | Character | Credits per 5s (480p / 720p / 1080p) |
|---|---|---|
| Seedance Fast | Natural motion, cheap trial passes | 15 / 20 / 45 |
| Seedance Pro | Smooth premium finish; accepts an end frame | 25 / 50 / 120 |
| Hailuo | Stylized energy, 6s clips | 30 / 30 / 50 |

A sting wants 3–5 seconds; Seedance prices scale per second, so a 3s trial is cheaper than the 5s table price. **Always run a trial on Seedance Fast at 480p first** - a drifted glyph shows at any resolution, and discovering it for 15 credits beats discovering it for 120. Finish on Seedance Pro for smooth, premium motion, or Hailuo when the brand wants visible energy.

Seedance Pro's end-frame conditioning is the sting cheat code: supply the **same plate as both first and last frame**, and the clip is forced to end exactly on the locked mark - displace-and-snap and shadow-retreat treatments resolve to pixel-perfect registration by construction. Use it whenever the finish runs on Pro.

State the trial cost and the finish cost when proposing the sting, and get agreement on the ladder rather than on one number.

## Prompt skeleton

```text
The mark at center is built of separate rigid shapes. Each shape <shifts 4mm | rotates 8 degrees | drops slightly> in turn, holds its offset, then all snap back into exact registration together with one small overshoot, and hold still. Static camera, plain unchanged background, constant realtime speed, no speed ramps. The mark's shapes keep their exact drawn form throughout - nothing redraws, warps, stretches, or morphs. No added text, letters, taglines, logos, watermarks, or extra graphics.
```

For a light-driven treatment, swap the first two sentences: `A single hard highlight travels left to right across the mark at center at a constant rate, igniting each element as it passes and leaving it softly lit. The mark and camera stay completely still.`

## Inspect it letter by letter

A mark that is 95% right is 100% wrong. Compare the first and last frames at full size, glyph by glyph:

- Every character is the correct character, none added, dropped, or duplicated.
- Stroke weights and spacing match the plate - no collisions, no gaps.
- Counters (the enclosed shapes in a, e, o, R) are open and correctly shaped.
- No warp, skew, or perspective change that was not asked for.
- No tagline, URL, or watermark was invented.
- The mark is as sharp in the last frame as the first.

Any failure is a retake, not a note. If three attempts all drift the mark: check the plate at full resolution first (a soft or upscaled mark cannot survive - the plate is the ceiling), then reduce ambition to a camera-locked, light-only treatment - the mark that never moves cannot be re-lettered.

## Reject a clip when

- Any glyph fails the letter-by-letter inspection above.
- The mark drifts, breathes, or shimmers between forms even though the treatment was light-only.
- The background changes, gains texture, or invents set dressing the plate did not have.
- The motion overshoots and never settles - a sting must end on a held, composed frame.
- New text or graphics appear anywhere in frame.

When placing the sting on a page: mute it, autoplay it, mark it `playsinline`, use the plate as the `poster` frame, and fall back to the plate under `prefers-reduced-motion`. The sting is an asset; the page decides when it plays.
